question: What proportion of adults with a hip fracture have a physiotherapy assessment and are mobilised the day after surgery, unless medically or surgically contraindicated?
why: Early mobilisation after hip fracture reduces chest infection, pressure damage and loss of independence, but delayed first mobilisation is common when therapy staffing does not cover weekends. No closed-loop audit of day-after-surgery physiotherapy mobilisation for hip fracture inpatients has been published in the library; related fragility-fracture physiotherapy timing has been audited [ONA-157] but that audit explicitly excludes hip fracture.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.1 (2011)
standard.wording: Offer people a physiotherapy assessment and, unless medically or surgically contraindicated, mobilisation on the day after surgery.

pass: Physiotherapy assessment documented and mobilisation attempted on the calendar day after surgery, or a documented medical/surgical contraindication recorded that day
population: Inclusion: all adults admitted with a hip fracture who had surgery. Exclusion: patients managed non-operatively, patients who died before day 1, patients discharged before day 1
sample: 40 consecutive adults having hip fracture surgery over the last 2-3 months, from the hip fracture register/NHFD extract
data_source: Physiotherapy notes, NHFD/trauma database, nursing observations, EPR mobility entries
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'day-1 physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation attempt: yes/no, reason if no' field to the hip fracture pathway proforma, and extend weekend physiotherapy cover to match the day-of-week distribution of surgery.
reaudit: 8-10 weeks later, same template and sample size, after the weekend cover change
close_loop: Present at the trauma/orthogeriatric MDT meeting and the therapy department governance meeting; if the change works, embed the field permanently in the hip fracture EPR pathway and report day-1 mobilisation rates alongside other NHFD key performance indicators.
evidence: [ONA-157] fragility fractures other than hip: BOAST day-after-surgery physiotherapy standard used as a comparable, unaudited-for-hip-fracture criterion
[ONA-008] hip fracture nerve block within 4 hours: shows the corpus already tracks other NHFD-linked timing indicators for this population
pitfalls: Weekend and bank holiday surgery has no physiotherapy cover → negotiate 7-day therapy rotas with the therapy lead before cycle 1
Contraindications are recorded inconsistently or not at all → add a mandatory free-text reason field so 'not mobilised' always has an explanation
Small numbers if only complete NHFD-linked cases are used → include all operated hip fractures, not just those with full NHFD data
Definitions of 'mobilised' vary between a sit-out and a walk → agree and print one operational definition before data collection starts
Gains fade once weekend cover reverts → make the rota change permanent in the therapy job plan, not a temporary trial
pearls: Recruit a physiotherapy team lead and the orthogeriatrician as joint audit leads so the change survives staff rotation
Agree the operational definition of 'mobilised' (sit to stand, transfer, or walk) with therapy staff before collecting data
Use the existing NHFD extract to identify the sample quickly rather than searching EPR from scratch
Feed results back to individual consultants and therapy shifts, not just as a trust-wide average, to drive local ownership
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from the NHFD extract and physiotherapy notes

question: What proportion of hip fracture inpatients are mobilised at least once a day with regular physiotherapy review throughout their acute stay?
why: A single day-1 assessment does not guarantee ongoing rehabilitation; patients can be assessed once and then left without daily mobilisation, especially over busy weekends. No closed-loop audit of ongoing (beyond day 1) daily mobilisation frequency for hip fracture inpatients has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.2 (2011)
standard.wording: Offer people mobilisation at least once a day and ensure regular physiotherapy review.

pass: Documented mobilisation attempt on every day of the acute admission and at least 3 physiotherapy reviews per week until discharge or rehabilitation-ready
population: Inclusion: adults who had hip fracture surgery and remained an inpatient for at least 5 days. Exclusion: patients who died, were transferred out, or were discharged within 4 days
sample: 40 consecutive hip fracture inpatients with a length of stay of 5 days or more over the last 3 months
data_source: Physiotherapy daily entries, nursing mobility charts, EPR therapy task list
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'mobilised today: yes/no, reason if no' task to the hip fracture ward's electronic therapy list so a missed day is visible on the ward board round, and set a weekend physiotherapy rota matched to the ward's bed numbers.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthogeriatric MDT and therapy governance meeting; embed the daily task list permanently if missed-day rates fall.
evidence: [ONA-157] day-after-surgery physiotherapy for other fragility fractures: comparable single-timepoint indicator, not the ongoing-frequency question asked here
pitfalls: Weekend staffing gaps are the commonest cause of missed days → confirm weekend rotas before starting
Patients who become medically unwell mid-stay may appropriately miss a day → record a reason rather than counting every miss as a failure
Documentation of 'seen but not mobilised' is easy to miss in free-text notes → use a structured daily tick box, not narrative notes, for data extraction
Staff may see this as a workload-driven target rather than a patient outcome → present length-of-stay and discharge-destination data alongside mobilisation rates
Long lengths of stay reduce the eligible sample → extend the collection window if fewer than 40 eligible patients are found in 3 months
pearls: Link this audit to the existing hip fracture pathway audit so both cycles use the same case list
Ask ward physiotherapists to flag missed days themselves during data collection rather than relying on retrospective note review
Present results by day of week to show where gaps cluster
Keep the daily task list active after the project team disbands by building it into the ward's standard operating procedure
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from daily therapy and nursing records

question: What proportion of COPD inpatients with excessive sputum production are taught active cycle of breathing techniques or positive expiratory pressure device use by a physiotherapist?
why: Sputum retention prolongs COPD exacerbations and increases the risk of further infection, but airway clearance teaching is easily missed when respiratory physiotherapy capacity is limited. No audit of airway clearance technique teaching for COPD inpatients with excessive sputum has been published in the library; pulmonary rehabilitation referral after discharge has been audited separately [NNA-395].

standard.source: NICE NG115 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s, recommendation 1.2.101 (2004, amended 2018)
standard.wording: If people have excessive sputum, they should be taught: how to use positive expiratory pressure devices, active cycle of breathing techniques.

pass: Documented physiotherapy teaching of active cycle of breathing techniques and/or a positive expiratory pressure device before discharge, for a patient with recorded excessive sputum
population: Inclusion: adults admitted with an acute exacerbation of COPD and a nursing or medical note of excessive/purulent sputum. Exclusion: patients unable to participate (for example, reduced consciousness) or who die before physiotherapy review
sample: 40 consecutive COPD exacerbation admissions with documented excessive sputum over the last 3 months
data_source: Admission clerking, nursing notes, physiotherapy referral and treatment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'excessive sputum: yes/no' to the COPD admission bundle so a yes automatically generates a same-day respiratory physiotherapy referral, with airway clearance teaching and a PEP device as the default action.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the respiratory directorate and physiotherapy governance meetings; embed the automatic referral trigger in the COPD admission order set if it works.
evidence: [NNA-395] pulmonary rehabilitation referral after COPD exacerbation discharge: an adjacent but distinct COPD physiotherapy indicator, not airway clearance teaching during the admission
pitfalls: Sputum volume/purulence is not always documented in a structured field → agree a simple nursing prompt ('sputum: none/scant/moderate/copious') before starting
Weekend admissions may wait 2-3 days for physiotherapy review → record the referral-to-teaching interval, not just whether teaching ever happened
Patients too breathless or drowsy to learn a technique are wrongly counted as failures → add an exclusion/deferred category with a reason
Teaching without device issue undermines the fix → audit both teaching and equipment provision separately
Staff may see this as duplicating existing physiotherapy referral practice → show baseline data first to demonstrate the gap
pearls: Involve the respiratory physiotherapy team lead in designing the sputum documentation prompt so it fits their existing workflow
Keep a small stock of PEP devices on the respiratory ward so teaching is not delayed by equipment ordering
Use the same COPD admission cohort as any existing pulmonary rehabilitation referral audit to save data collection time
Report results to the wider medical team, since sputum documentation is a doctor and nurse responsibility as much as a physiotherapy one
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from admission and physiotherapy notes

question: What proportion of hospital inpatients assessed as being at risk of falls are encouraged and supported to remain physically active during their admission?
why: Bed rest and reduced activity during a hospital stay increase deconditioning and paradoxically raise falls risk after discharge, yet 'stay in bed to be safe' remains common ward practice. No audit of inpatient physical activity promotion as part of falls prevention has been published in the library; falls medication review and comprehensive assessment referral have been audited separately [ONA-014, ONA-016, ONA-130].

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.3.19 (2025)
standard.wording: Encourage people to remain active during their hospital stay by: reassuring them that they can still get up and do not need to restrict their activity (unless they have been advised not to) and helping them to be less sedentary and more active, for example, encouraging them to get out of bed, get dressed and regularly stand up and walk around and for people able to exercise, look for opportunities to encourage physical activity that addresses the person's risk of falls, such as balance, coordination, strength and power.

pass: Documented physiotherapy or nursing encouragement of activity (getting up, walking, or an exercise component) on at least 3 of the first 5 inpatient days for a patient identified as at risk of falls
population: Inclusion: adults aged 65 and over admitted to a general medical or older people's ward with a documented falls risk. Exclusion: patients on strict bed rest for a documented clinical reason, patients discharged within 48 hours
sample: 40 consecutive falls-risk inpatients over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Nursing mobility charts, physiotherapy notes, ward activity boards
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a daily 'up and active today: yes/no, reason if no' box to the ward activity/mobility chart, with a prompt for a balance or strength exercise when appropriate, replacing any blanket 'bed rest for safety' default.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the ward safety huddle and falls steering group; if activity rates improve, embed the daily prompt in the standard nursing and therapy documentation.
evidence: [ONA-014] falls medicines review before discharge, [ONA-016] comprehensive falls assessment referral, [ONA-130] FLS falls risk assessment: related falls-prevention audits that do not measure inpatient activity promotion
pitfalls: 'Falls risk' documentation is inconsistent across wards → agree a single falls risk flag (for example, a falls risk assessment score) before starting
Staff may equate encouraging activity with increased falls, causing reluctance → share evidence that inactivity, not appropriate mobilisation, drives post-discharge falls and deconditioning
Bed rest reasons are not always documented → make a reason mandatory whenever activity is withheld
Ward staffing pressure limits time for supervised walking → recruit ward-based therapy assistants for regular short mobilisation rounds
Improvement may not be sustained once the audit team stops checking → build the prompt into existing nursing handover checklists
pearls: Frame this as a deconditioning-prevention project, which tends to get more staff buy-in than a pure falls-prevention framing
Recruit a ward sister and a physiotherapist as joint champions before cycle 1
Use existing 'sit up, get dressed, keep moving' campaign materials rather than creating new posters from scratch
Track length of stay alongside activity rates, since the intervention is expected to reduce it
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from nursing and therapy charts

question: What proportion of stroke patients receive at least 3 hours of needs-based, multidisciplinary rehabilitation therapy on at least 5 days of the week?
why: Rehabilitation intensity is strongly linked to functional recovery after stroke, but therapy staffing and weekend cover often fall short of the recommended intensity. No closed-loop audit of stroke rehabilitation intensity against the current NICE standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.16 (2023)
standard.wording: Offer needs-based rehabilitation to people after stroke. This should be for at least 3 hours a day, on at least 5 days of the week, and cover a range of multidisciplinary therapy including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy.

pass: Total documented therapy time (physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy combined) is at least 3 hours on at least 5 of 7 days during a defined week of the stroke unit stay, or a documented reason recorded when the person is unable or unwilling to participate at that level
population: Inclusion: adults on the acute or rehabilitation stroke unit for at least 7 days. Exclusion: patients receiving end-of-life care, patients transferred within the first week
sample: 40 consecutive stroke unit patients with a stay of 7 days or more over the last 3 months
data_source: Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy timed treatment logs, SSNAP data extract
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a shared electronic therapy timesheet across physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy that automatically totals daily minutes per patient and flags days below the 3-hour target for review at the daily board round.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT meeting and to SSNAP data leads; embed the shared timesheet permanently and report intensity rates as a standing SSNAP-linked local metric if it improves.
pitfalls: Each therapy discipline may record time in a different system, making totals hard to combine → agree one shared recording format before starting
Weekend and bank holiday staffing typically falls below weekday levels → report weekday and weekend rates separately
Patients who genuinely cannot tolerate 3 hours (fatigue, reduced consciousness) are miscounted as failures → record a clinical reason field
Recording therapy time without documenting content risks gaming the metric → also spot-check that time reflects active, needs-based rehabilitation, not passive contact
Improvement may fade if extra weekend staffing is temporary → secure a recurring weekend therapy rota, not a short-term trial
pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing SSNAP data collection processes to avoid duplicating data entry
Agree the shared timesheet format with all three therapy disciplines before cycle 1 so ownership is shared, not imposed
Present intensity data alongside length of stay and functional outcome scores to show the clinical case for investment
Nominate a stroke unit therapy lead to keep the timesheet running after the initial audit team moves on
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from combined therapy timesheets

question: What proportion of patients receiving a structured rehabilitation programme on the ward after critical illness have a functional assessment covering physical, sensory, communication and activities-of-daily-living dimensions completed before hospital discharge?
why: Physical and cognitive problems after critical illness are easy to miss once patients move to a general ward, and unassessed needs are not referred on after discharge. No audit of the pre-discharge functional assessment for post-critical-illness rehabilitation has been published in the library; ICU rehabilitation goal-setting and ward handover have been audited separately [NNA-056, NNA-057].

standard.source: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.20 (2009)
standard.wording: Before discharging patients who were receiving the individualised structured rehabilitation programme during ward-based care (recommendation 1.15): perform a functional assessment which should include the following physical and non-physical dimensions... assess the impact of the outcomes from the functional assessment on the patient's activities of daily living and participation; based on the functional assessment, review, update and agree the rehabilitation goals with the patient.

pass: A documented functional assessment covering physical, sensory, communication, and activities-of-daily-living dimensions, completed and the rehabilitation goals reviewed, within 72 hours before discharge from hospital
population: Inclusion: adults who had a critical care stay of 4 days or more and received a ward-based structured rehabilitation programme. Exclusion: patients who died before discharge, patients discharged directly from critical care without a ward stay
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients discharged from hospital over the last 3-4 months, identified from the critical care outreach or follow-up log
data_source: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy functional assessment notes, ward discharge documentation, critical care follow-up records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory pre-discharge functional assessment template (covering physical, sensory, communication and ADL dimensions) to the EPR for any patient flagged as having received ICU-linked ward rehabilitation, which must be completed before the discharge summary can be finalised.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the critical care outreach and rehabilitation MDT meeting; embed the mandatory template in the discharge workflow if completion rates improve.
evidence: [NNA-056] rehabilitation goals agreed within 4 days of ICU admission, [NNA-057] rehabilitation plan included in ward handover: related but earlier-stage CG83 indicators that do not audit the pre-discharge functional assessment
pitfalls: Patients who move wards or hospitals before discharge are hard to track → use the critical care outreach follow-up list as the sampling frame
ADL impact is often assessed informally without documentation → provide a short structured template rather than relying on free text
Busy discharge processes can push the assessment out of the pre-discharge window → set a hard 72-hour trigger on the EPR
Onward referral (community rehabilitation, GP, outpatient follow-up) is easy to omit even when the assessment is done → audit referral completion as a separate field
Staff turnover on rotating ward teams may not know which patients had a critical care stay → flag ICU-linked patients on the ward handover board
pearls: Use the critical care follow-up service, where one exists, to help identify the sample and check onward referrals were received
Involve both physiotherapy and occupational therapy in designing the shared functional assessment template so it captures both disciplines' domains
Present findings jointly to critical care and general ward teams, since responsibility is shared between them
Keep the mandatory EPR trigger active permanently rather than as a time-limited pilot
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from therapy and discharge notes

question: What proportion of patients at risk of long-term physical or psychological problems after critical illness are offered a structured, supported self-directed rehabilitation manual for at least 6 weeks after critical care discharge?
why: Many patients leave critical care with unmet rehabilitation needs that only become apparent weeks later, when formal therapy contact has usually stopped. No audit of self-directed rehabilitation manual provision after critical illness has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.18 (2009)
standard.wording: Based on clinical judgement and the individual patient's rehabilitation needs, consider offering a structured and supported self-directed rehabilitation manual for at least 6 weeks after discharge from critical care, as part of the individualised, structured rehabilitation programme.

pass: Documented offer of a structured, supported self-directed rehabilitation manual, with a named coordinating healthcare professional, for a patient identified as at risk of physical or non-physical morbidity
population: Inclusion: adults identified as at risk of physical or non-physical morbidity on the short clinical assessment during or after critical care. Exclusion: patients who died, patients discharged directly to end-of-life or palliative care
sample: 30-40 consecutive at-risk patients discharged from critical care over the last 3-4 months
data_source: Critical care discharge summary, ward and outreach follow-up notes, rehabilitation programme documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'self-directed rehabilitation manual offered: yes/no, coordinator named' as a mandatory field on the critical care discharge summary template, with the manual and coordinator contact details included in the discharge pack as standard.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the critical care follow-up clinic and outreach team meeting; embed the discharge pack change permanently if offer rates rise.
pitfalls: Which patients count as 'at risk' is subjective without a documented short clinical assessment → use table 1 of CG83 as a structured checklist
The manual may be offered but not actually coordinated for 6 weeks → audit both the offer and the presence of a named coordinator
Patients discharged out of area lose follow-up continuity → record discharge destination and adapt the coordination plan accordingly
Staff may not know the manual exists if it has not previously been used locally → confirm a manual is available and staff are briefed before cycle 1
Low baseline awareness can make the first cycle very low, discouraging staff → present it as a baseline-setting exercise, not a failure
pearls: Base the manual on a published, validated self-directed rehabilitation programme rather than creating one from scratch
Identify a single named critical care outreach practitioner to coordinate all manual referrals so responsibility does not diffuse
Combine this with the pre-discharge functional assessment audit, since both draw on the same discharge population
Ask patients or carers at the 2-3 month functional reassessment whether they received and used the manual, to check the fix is actually working, not just documented
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from discharge documentation

question: What proportion of people having a comprehensive falls assessment have their gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength formally assessed as part of it?
why: Comprehensive falls assessments are often completed as a tick-box medical review without the physical components that identify a treatable cause, particularly muscle weakness and balance impairment. No audit of physiotherapy-relevant domains within the comprehensive falls assessment has been published in the library; falls medication review and FLS falls screening have been audited separately [ONA-014, ONA-130].

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.2.2 (2025)
standard.wording: Include the following assessments and examinations (where appropriate) in the comprehensive falls assessment to identify the person's individual fall risk factors: ...Gait, balance and mobility, and muscle strength assessment...

pass: Documented assessment of gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength (for example, using a timed up-and-go, Berg balance score, or equivalent structured tool) recorded as part of the comprehensive falls assessment
population: Inclusion: adults having a comprehensive falls assessment in hospital or in a community falls service. Exclusion: assessments explicitly limited to a single domain by clinical necessity (for example, acute medical instability)
sample: 40 consecutive comprehensive falls assessments over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Falls clinic or ward comprehensive falls assessment documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add mandatory gait, balance and muscle strength fields, with a named structured tool, to the comprehensive falls assessment template, and route any assessment lacking physiotherapy input to a physiotherapist before it is signed off as complete.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the falls steering group and therapy governance meeting; embed the mandatory fields permanently if completion rates improve.
evidence: [ONA-014] falls-focused medicines review, [ONA-130] FLS falls risk screen: related falls assessment components that do not audit the physical/physiotherapy domains specifically
pitfalls: Non-physiotherapy staff completing the assessment may skip physical domains they feel less confident measuring → provide a simple, validated tool with brief training
Different services may use different tools, making results hard to compare over time → agree one tool trust-wide before cycle 1
Acutely unwell patients cannot safely be assessed for gait or balance → record a deferred/not-yet-safe category rather than a fail
Duplication of effort if physiotherapy and medical teams assess separately without sharing results → use one shared assessment form
Improvement gained during the audit period may lapse without an embedded prompt → build the fields into the permanent electronic template, not a paper checklist
pearls: Recruit a falls service physiotherapist as joint audit lead alongside the geriatrician or falls coordinator
Choose a quick, validated tool (for example, timed up-and-go) that non-specialist staff can be trained to use in one session
Present results split by setting (ward versus falls clinic) since completion rates often differ
Use the audit as an opportunity to formalise physiotherapy input into every comprehensive falls assessment pathway, not just document it
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from falls assessment documentation

question: What proportion of adults identified through a comprehensive falls assessment as needing a home hazard assessment have one carried out using a validated tool, by an occupational therapist or a supervised trained assistant?
why: Home hazards are a modifiable falls risk factor, but home visits are resource-intensive and can be skipped when occupational therapy capacity is stretched. No audit of home hazard assessment completion against the current NICE falls standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendations 1.3.5-1.3.6 (2025)
standard.wording: Offer a home hazard assessment and intervention using a validated tool. Consider having the home hazard assessment and intervention from recommendation 1.3.5 carried out by an occupational therapist. If an occupational therapist does not carry out the assessment and intervention, it may be done by: an appropriately trained healthcare professional or an appropriately trained therapy assistant or technician, with supervision from an appropriately trained healthcare professional.

pass: A home hazard assessment using a named validated tool, completed by an occupational therapist or a supervised trained assistant, with documented intervention where hazards were found
population: Inclusion: adults offered comprehensive falls management following a comprehensive falls assessment. Exclusion: people who decline the assessment, people who move into 24-hour care before it can be arranged
sample: 40 consecutive adults referred for a home hazard assessment over the last 3 months
data_source: Occupational therapy referral and home visit records, falls service caseload
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set a target referral-to-home-visit interval on the occupational therapy caseload system, with an automated overdue flag, and train falls-service therapy assistants to deliver supervised home hazard assessments using a single named validated tool.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the falls service and occupational therapy team meetings; embed the caseload overdue flag permanently if waiting times fall.
pitfalls: Home visits are cancelled if the patient is not in, wasting capacity → confirm appointments by phone the day before
Different therapists may use different or no validated tools → agree and print a single tool before cycle 1
Long waiting lists mean many referrals are still open at audit close → report both completion rate and median waiting time
Assistants delivering the assessment without documented supervision breaches the standard even if the visit happens → make supervision sign-off a mandatory field
Gains from extra capacity may be temporary if funded only for the audit period → seek a recurring establishment change if waiting times improve
pearls: Use the falls service's existing caseload system rather than building a new tracking spreadsheet
Agree with occupational therapy leadership which validated tool to standardise on before starting data collection
Recruit a therapy assistant champion, since much of the extra capacity this audit is likely to need will come from supervised assistants
Report waiting time trends monthly to keep momentum after the formal audit report is presented
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from occupational therapy caseload records

question: What proportion of people in the community who have fallen once in the last year, with a gait or balance impairment but no other risk factor, are offered a home hazard assessment using a validated tool?
why: People with a single fall and a gait or balance impairment do not meet criteria for full comprehensive falls management, so their home hazard risk can be overlooked entirely. No audit of home hazard assessment for this single-fall community population has been published in the library; comprehensive inpatient falls management has been audited elsewhere in the library [ONA-016].

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendations 1.3.13-1.3.14 (2025)
standard.wording: Consider a home hazard assessment and intervention using a validated tool. Consider having the home hazard assessment and intervention from recommendation 1.3.13 carried out by an occupational therapist. If an occupational therapist does not carry out the assessment and intervention, it may be done by: an appropriately trained healthcare professional or an appropriately trained therapy assistant or technician, with supervision from an appropriately trained healthcare professional.

pass: Documented offer of a home hazard assessment using a validated tool for a person with a single fall in the last year and a documented gait or balance impairment, who does not otherwise meet comprehensive falls management criteria
population: Inclusion: adults aged 65 and over in community or primary care settings with one fall in the last year and a documented gait or balance impairment on assessment. Exclusion: people meeting comprehensive falls management criteria
sample: 30-40 consecutive people identified from GP falls searches or community falls service referrals over the last 3-4 months
data_source: GP records, community falls service referral log, gait/balance assessment notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'single fall with gait/balance impairment: home hazard assessment offered?' prompt to the GP falls template so this group is not missed between comprehensive falls management and no action at all.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the primary care network falls meeting and community occupational therapy service; embed the GP template prompt permanently if uptake improves.
evidence: [ONA-016] comprehensive falls assessment referral for fracture patients: audits a different, higher-risk falls population than the single-fall group considered here
pitfalls: This population is easy to miss because it falls between 'no action needed' and 'full comprehensive assessment' → make the eligibility criteria explicit on the GP template
GPs may not routinely document gait or balance impairment structurally → provide a simple one-line documentation prompt
Community occupational therapy capacity for lower-priority referrals may be limited → agree a realistic waiting time target with the service before cycle 1
Patients may decline a home visit they see as unnecessary after a single fall → record declines separately from missed offers
Findings may not generalise if only one GP practice is audited → sample from more than one practice within the primary care network
pearls: Work with the primary care network falls lead to identify the sample via a coded search rather than manual note review
Keep the referral pathway simple (a single click or form) to make it easy for GPs to use during a routine consultation
Track whether hazards found at these lower-risk assessments still lead to meaningful interventions, not just a completed form
Share results with the practice, since GPs are the ones who need to change referral behaviour
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from GP and community therapy records

question: What proportion of stroke patients with documented communication or cognitive needs have joint occupational therapy, physiotherapy or speech and language therapy sessions arranged, rather than separate uncoordinated therapy contacts?
why: People with communication or cognitive impairment after stroke can struggle to engage with therapy delivered by a single discipline in isolation, but joint sessions require active coordination that is easy to lose amid competing caseloads. No audit of joint therapy session arrangements for stroke patients with communication or cognitive needs has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.21 (2023)
standard.wording: Make special arrangements for people after stroke who have communication or cognitive needs (for example, by holding joint speech and language therapy and physiotherapy sessions for those with communication difficulties).

pass: At least one documented joint therapy session (two or more disciplines present together) recorded in the multidisciplinary notes for a stroke patient with a documented communication or cognitive need
population: Inclusion: adults on the stroke unit with a documented communication or cognitive impairment on initial assessment. Exclusion: patients discharged or who die within 72 hours of admission
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible stroke unit patients over the last 3 months
data_source: Multidisciplinary team notes, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy treatment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a weekly 'joint session planned: which disciplines, when' slot to the stroke MDT therapy timetable for every patient flagged with a communication or cognitive need, agreed at the weekly MDT meeting.
target: ≥70% of eligible patients having at least one joint session per week
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT meeting; embed the weekly joint-session planning slot permanently in the MDT agenda if uptake improves.
pitfalls: Coordinating diaries across three disciplines is logistically difficult → fix a single weekly slot in advance rather than arranging ad hoc
Joint sessions may happen informally without being documented as such → add a specific joint-session tick box to the shared MDT note
Staff shortages in any one discipline can cancel joint sessions first → monitor cancellation reasons separately from non-arrangement
Patients who are too fatigued for a longer joint session may be excluded inappropriately → allow a shorter, still-joint session to count
The fix may lapse once the weekly MDT champion moves on → build the joint-session slot into the standing MDT meeting template
pearls: Agree the joint-session slot with all three therapy leads before cycle 1, not just the audit team
Use the stroke unit's existing weekly MDT meeting to plan the following week's joint sessions rather than a separate coordination meeting
Track patient and carer feedback on joint sessions, since this is often the strongest driver of continued staff engagement
Keep the documentation simple (a tick box plus disciplines present) so it does not become a burden that gets skipped
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from stroke unit MDT and therapy notes

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients considered for early supported discharge have their medical stability, mental capacity to participate, and ability to transfer and mobilise short distances formally assessed and documented before the decision is made?
why: Early supported discharge after hip fracture depends on occupational therapy and physiotherapy jointly confirming specific functional criteria, but the decision can be made informally without all criteria being checked and recorded. No audit of documented early supported discharge criteria for hip fracture patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.8.4 (2011)
standard.wording: Consider early supported discharge as part of the Hip Fracture Programme, provided the Hip Fracture Programme multidisciplinary team remains involved, and the person: is medically stable and has the mental ability to participate in continued rehabilitation and is able to transfer and mobilise short distances and has not yet achieved their full rehabilitation potential, as discussed with the person, carer and family.

pass: All four criteria (medical stability, mental ability to participate, ability to transfer/mobilise short distances, discussion with patient/carer/family) documented as assessed before an early supported discharge decision is recorded
population: Inclusion: adults with a hip fracture discharged via an early supported discharge pathway. Exclusion: patients discharged to their normal place of residence without early supported discharge, patients who die as an inpatient
sample: 30-40 consecutive hip fracture patients discharged via early supported discharge over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Orthogeriatric MDT notes, occupational therapy and physiotherapy assessment records, discharge planning documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory four-item checklist (medical stability, mental capacity, transfer/mobility, discussion) to the early supported discharge decision form, which must be completed by occupational therapy and physiotherapy jointly before the discharge is booked.
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the orthogeriatric MDT and community early supported discharge team meeting; embed the checklist permanently in the discharge decision workflow if documentation improves.
pitfalls: Criteria may be genuinely assessed but not documented in one place → create a single decision form rather than relying on scattered entries
Time pressure to free beds can lead to the decision being made before all four criteria are checked → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge order
Mental capacity to participate in rehabilitation can be confused with formal mental capacity for decision-making → define the term clearly in the checklist
Family discussion may happen by phone and go unrecorded → add a simple 'discussed with: date, method' field
Early supported discharge teams outside the acute trust may not see this audit as their responsibility → involve the community team from the outset
pearls: Design the four-item checklist jointly with occupational therapy, physiotherapy and the early supported discharge team so all parties recognise it
Pilot the checklist on a small number of patients before full rollout to iron out practical problems
Use the same case list as any hip fracture length-of-stay or readmission audit to show the checklist does not increase early readmission
Keep the checklist short (one page) so it is completed rather than bypassed under time pressure
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT and discharge records

question: What proportion of patients receiving a pre-discharge functional assessment after critical illness have the impact on their activities of daily living formally assessed as part of it?
why: Physical recovery from critical illness is often tracked, but the day-to-day functional impact on washing, dressing, cooking and mobility at home is less consistently assessed, delaying appropriate occupational therapy support after discharge. No audit of the activities-of-daily-living component of the pre-discharge functional assessment after critical illness has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.20 (2009)
standard.wording: Before discharging patients who were receiving the individualised structured rehabilitation programme during ward-based care...perform a functional assessment...assess the impact of the outcomes from the functional assessment on the patient's activities of daily living and participation.

pass: Documented assessment of the impact on activities of daily living (for example, washing, dressing, cooking, mobility at home) as part of the pre-discharge functional assessment, with any identified need referred on
population: Inclusion: adults who had a critical care stay of 4 days or more and a ward-based structured rehabilitation programme. Exclusion: patients discharged directly from critical care, patients who die before discharge
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3-4 months
data_source: Occupational therapy functional assessment notes, ward discharge documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory occupational-therapy-led ADL impact section to the pre-discharge functional assessment template, with a built-in referral pathway for any identified need.
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the critical care follow-up and occupational therapy team meetings; embed the mandatory ADL section permanently if completion rates improve.
pitfalls: ADL impact may be assumed rather than formally assessed → require a structured tool or checklist, not a general impression
Occupational therapy capacity may be limited on general wards → prioritise ICU-linked patients on the daily occupational therapy referral list
Identified needs may not lead to an actual referral → audit referral completion as a separate outcome, not just assessment completion
Patients discharged to a care home may have needs met differently → record discharge destination to interpret results correctly
A low baseline in the first cycle may discourage staff → present it as identifying an opportunity, not blaming individuals
pearls: Combine this audit with the wider CG83 functional assessment audit to avoid double data collection
Involve ward-based occupational therapists directly in designing the ADL section so it matches their normal assessment style
Track discharge destination and any early readmission alongside ADL assessment completion to show the clinical value of the fix
Keep a named occupational therapy lead responsible for the mandatory field after the initial project ends
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from occupational therapy and discharge notes

question: What proportion of hospital inpatients diagnosed with delirium have documented reorientation, effective communication and a suitable care environment provided as part of their initial management?
why: Reorientation and environmental measures are the first-line, non-drug treatment for delirium, but they are easy to omit from documentation compared with medication changes, and occupational therapy input into a suitable environment is often absent. No audit of the reorientation and environment component of delirium management has been published in the library; delirium documentation in discharge summaries has been audited separately [NNA-134, ONA-005].

standard.source: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management, recommendation 1.7.2 (2010)
standard.wording: Ensure effective communication and reorientation (for example explaining where the person is, who they are and what your role is) and provide reassurance for people diagnosed with delirium. Consider involving family, friends and carers to help with this. Provide a suitable care environment.

pass: Documented reorientation and communication measures and a suitable care environment (for example, clear signage, visible clock, consistent staff, reduced noise or a side room where appropriate) recorded within 24 hours of a delirium diagnosis
population: Inclusion: adults with a new diagnosis of delirium during the admission. Exclusion: patients who die or are transferred within 24 hours of diagnosis
sample: 40 consecutive inpatients newly diagnosed with delirium over the last 3 months
data_source: Nursing and medical notes, delirium care bundle documentation, occupational therapy notes where involved
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a delirium care bundle to the EPR that is triggered automatically by a positive delirium screening tool, with mandatory reorientation, family involvement and environment fields, and a same-day occupational therapy referral option.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the delirium/dementia steering group and ward safety huddle; embed the automatic care bundle trigger permanently if documentation rates improve.
evidence: [NNA-134] delirium recorded in discharge summary, [ONA-005] delirium written in orthogeriatric discharge summary: audit documentation of the diagnosis at discharge, not the reorientation and environment management during the admission
pitfalls: Reorientation is often done verbally but never written down → provide a simple tick-box bundle rather than relying on narrative notes
Ward layout and side-room availability may limit what environmental changes are realistically possible → record what was feasible given bed availability
Occupational therapy may not routinely be involved in delirium care on general wards → create a clear referral trigger rather than assuming automatic involvement
Family involvement is harder to document when visiting hours or distance limit contact → record attempts to involve family, not only successful involvement
Care bundle completion can become a box-ticking exercise disconnected from actual care → spot-check a sample against direct observation or family feedback
pearls: Build on any existing delirium screening tool already used on the ward rather than introducing a separate process
Involve a ward-based occupational therapist in designing the environment checklist items so they are practical for the ward layout
Present results alongside length of stay and falls data, since delirium management affects both
Nominate delirium link nurses on each ward to keep the care bundle embedded after the audit team's involvement ends
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from nursing and medical notes

question: What proportion of adults at high risk of a heel pressure ulcer have an individualised offloading strategy discussed with them and documented in their care plan?
why: Heel pressure ulcers are common, painful and slow to heal, but offloading strategies (heel-lift devices, boots, positioning) are less consistently planned and documented than general repositioning schedules. No audit of individualised heel offloading strategy documentation has been published in the library; general pressure ulcer risk assessment and whole-body repositioning frequency have been audited separately [NNA-272, NNA-273, ONA-153].

standard.source: NICE CG179 Pressure ulcers: prevention and management, recommendation 1.1.15 (2014)
standard.wording: Discuss with adults at high risk of developing a heel pressure ulcer and, where appropriate, their family or carers, a strategy to offload heel pressure, as part of their individualised care plan.

pass: A documented, individualised heel offloading strategy (device named or positioning plan described) in the care plan of an adult identified as high risk of a heel pressure ulcer, with evidence of discussion with the patient or family
population: Inclusion: adults with a pressure ulcer risk assessment recording high risk and a documented heel-specific risk factor (for example, reduced mobility, diabetes, vascular disease). Exclusion: patients with an existing heel pressure ulcer already under active wound management with its own plan
sample: 40 consecutive high-risk adults identified over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Pressure ulcer risk assessment (SSKIN or equivalent), nursing and occupational therapy/tissue viability care plans
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'heel offloading strategy: device/plan, discussed with patient/family' field to the electronic SSKIN pressure ulcer care plan, triggered automatically when the risk assessment records high risk.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the tissue viability and ward safety huddle; embed the automatic SSKIN trigger permanently if documentation improves.
evidence: [NNA-272] pressure ulcer risk assessment within 6 hours of admission, [NNA-273] repositioning every 4 hours for high-risk adults: cover risk assessment and whole-body repositioning, not the heel-specific offloading strategy audited here
pitfalls: Heel offloading equipment (boots, wedges) may not be readily available on every ward → confirm equipment stock levels before cycle 1
General repositioning may be documented without a heel-specific plan → make heel offloading a distinct field, not implied by general repositioning notes
Patients may decline or remove offloading devices for comfort → record attempts and reasons for non-use rather than counting these as documentation failures
Occupational therapy or tissue viability capacity to review complex cases may be limited → prioritise review for the highest-risk patients first
Improvement may not be sustained if equipment runs out → agree a recurring equipment budget line with the tissue viability service
pearls: Involve tissue viability and occupational therapy jointly in designing the offloading field, since both disciplines contribute to equipment decisions
Use ward equipment champions to check heel-offloading device availability alongside data collection
Present pressure ulcer incidence data alongside documentation rates to show the clinical case for the change
Keep a simple picture-based guide at the bedside showing correct heel offloading positioning to support consistent practice
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from pressure ulcer care plans

question: What proportion of people having a comprehensive falls assessment have their footwear and foot condition assessed, with referral to podiatry when a problem is found?
why: Poor-fitting footwear and untreated foot problems are a recognised, easily-missed falls risk factor, and assessment of this domain is often skipped in favour of medical causes of falling. No audit of footwear and foot condition assessment with podiatry referral has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.2.2 (2025)
standard.wording: Include the following assessments and examinations (where appropriate) in the comprehensive falls assessment to identify the person's individual fall risk factors: ...Footwear and foot condition...

pass: Documented assessment of footwear and foot condition as part of the comprehensive falls assessment, with a podiatry referral made when a problem is identified
population: Inclusion: adults having a comprehensive falls assessment in hospital or a community falls service. Exclusion: assessments explicitly limited to a single domain by clinical necessity
sample: 40 consecutive comprehensive falls assessments over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Falls clinic or ward comprehensive falls assessment documentation, podiatry referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory footwear and foot condition field, with a direct one-click podiatry referral option, to the comprehensive falls assessment template.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the falls steering group, with podiatry service representation; embed the mandatory field and referral link permanently if completion rates improve.
pitfalls: Staff without podiatry training may feel unqualified to assess foot condition → provide a simple visual checklist (skin, nails, deformity, ulceration) rather than requiring specialist skills
Footwear may be assessed but not foot condition, or vice versa → record both as separate fields
Podiatry referral pathways may be unclear to non-podiatry staff → build a direct referral link into the assessment template
Referrals made may not be tracked to completion → add a follow-up field for whether the podiatry appointment happened
Low staff confidence in the first cycle may underestimate true completion → pair the audit with a short training session on the checklist
pearls: Ask the podiatry service to help design the simple foot-condition checklist so referrals are appropriately targeted
Combine this with the physiotherapy-led gait/balance/muscle strength audit, since both use the same comprehensive falls assessment template
Track how many referrals lead to a completed podiatry appointment, not just how many are made
Keep the referral link visible and easy to use so it survives staff turnover
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from falls assessment and podiatry referral records

question: What proportion of patients admitted to hospital with a stroke have their swallowing function screened before any oral food, fluid or medication is given, with action taken if a problem is identified?
why: Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death and prolonged stay after stroke, and delayed or absent swallow screening before oral intake remains a common preventable failure. No closed-loop audit of pre-oral-intake dysphagia screening after stroke has been published in the library; enteral tube placement timing after a failed swallow screen has been audited separately [NNA-125].

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.1 (2013)
standard.wording: When a person is admitted to hospital after stroke, screen for the following and, if problems are identified, take action as soon as possible to ensure their safety and comfort: signs of disorientation, how they should be positioned, swallowing function, how they move (for example, from a bed to a chair), pressure area risk, their continence, their communication, including their ability to understand and follow instructions and to convey their needs and wishes, their nutritional status and hydration.

pass: Documented swallow screen completed before any oral food, fluid or oral medication is given, and, if the screen is abnormal, a documented action (nil by mouth, modified diet, or referral for a specialist swallow assessment) recorded the same day
population: Inclusion: all adults admitted to hospital with a confirmed stroke. Exclusion: patients who are already nil by mouth for another reason on admission, patients receiving end-of-life care from arrival
sample: 40 consecutive stroke admissions over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Admission clerking, nursing observation charts, swallow screening tool documentation, drug chart timing
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make swallow screening a mandatory hard stop on the stroke admission order set, so no oral food, fluid or medication can be prescribed as 'oral' until the screen result is entered, with an automatic alert to speech and language therapy for any abnormal result.
reaudit: 8 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT meeting and SSNAP data review; embed the hard stop permanently in the EPR admission pathway if compliance improves.
evidence: [NNA-125] nasogastric tube placement within 24 hours of a failed swallow screen: audits the next step in the pathway, assuming a screen has already been done, not the screening step itself
pitfalls: Out-of-hours admissions may lack trained staff to perform the screen promptly → ensure all admitting nursing staff, not just stroke-unit staff, are trained in the screening tool
Medication is sometimes given orally before food or fluid screening is considered, and gets missed from data collection → explicitly define 'oral intake' to include medicines
A pass on a validated screening tool is not the same as a full speech and language therapy assessment → audit the screen, and separately track specialist assessment for those who fail
Staff may screen but delay recording the result, making timing hard to verify → use time-stamped electronic entries rather than paper charts where possible
Compliance may fall out of hours or at weekends → report weekday/weekend and in-hours/out-of-hours rates separately
pearls: Recruit the stroke unit matron and a speech and language therapist as joint audit leads
Use the trust's existing validated swallow screening tool rather than introducing a new one
Build the screening prompt into the same admission bundle used for other early stroke standards (glucose, positioning) to reduce duplication of effort
Report results at the same MDT meeting that reviews SSNAP performance so the audit becomes part of routine stroke unit governance
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from admission and nursing records

question: What proportion of stroke patients are screened for communication difficulties within 72 hours of the onset of stroke symptoms?
why: Communication problems after stroke affect a person's ability to consent to care and participate in rehabilitation, but screening is easy to overlook when it competes with physical assessments in the first days after stroke. No audit of the 72-hour communication screening standard after stroke has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.1 (2013)
standard.wording: Screen people for communication difficulties within 72 hours of onset of stroke symptoms.

pass: A documented communication screen, using the stroke service's standardised protocol, completed within 72 hours of the recorded onset of stroke symptoms
population: Inclusion: adults admitted with a confirmed stroke and a documented onset time. Exclusion: patients with an unknown or unwitnessed onset time, patients who die within 72 hours
sample: 40 consecutive stroke admissions with a documented onset time over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Stroke admission proforma, speech and language therapy assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 72-hour 'communication screen due' automated reminder to the stroke unit's electronic task list, triggered from the recorded onset time, with the screen built into the standard admission proforma.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT meeting; embed the automated 72-hour reminder permanently in the EPR if compliance rises.
pitfalls: Onset time is often estimated or unwitnessed, complicating the 72-hour calculation → record onset time precision (exact, estimated, unknown) as a separate field
Speech and language therapy weekend cover may be limited → report weekday versus weekend screening rates separately
Communication screening may be recorded informally in ward round notes rather than the standardised protocol → audit for use of the named protocol specifically, not any communication comment
Patients with severe dysphasia may be hard to screen definitively → record 'screen attempted, inconclusive' as a distinct category rather than a straightforward pass or fail
The 72-hour deadline can be missed simply through delayed transfer to the stroke unit → track time from onset to stroke unit arrival as well as to screening
pearls: Use the same stroke admission cohort as the swallow screening audit to minimise duplicate data collection
Agree a single standardised communication screening protocol with speech and language therapy before starting
Display the 72-hour deadline visibly on the stroke unit's patient board so nursing staff can prompt therapy teams
Report results alongside SSNAP communication indicators so the audit reinforces existing national reporting
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from stroke admission and therapy records

question: What proportion of stroke patients with dysphagia who are having modified food or fluids are regularly monitored and reassessed by a speech and language therapist until they are clinically stable?
why: Swallowing function often changes during a stroke admission, but once a modified diet is set, ongoing speech and language therapy reassessment can lapse, leaving patients on an outdated, overly restrictive or unsafe plan. No audit of ongoing dysphagia reassessment frequency for stroke patients on modified diets has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.11.9 (2013)
standard.wording: Healthcare professionals with relevant skills and training in the diagnosis, assessment and management of swallowing disorders should regularly monitor and reassess people with dysphagia after stroke who are having modified food and liquid until they are stable.

pass: At least one documented speech and language therapy reassessment per week for a patient on modified food or fluids, continuing until the diet is upgraded or the patient is discharged
population: Inclusion: adults after stroke on a modified (texture-modified or thickened fluid) diet for 7 days or more. Exclusion: patients on end-of-life comfort feeding, patients discharged within 7 days of starting modified diet
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3-4 months
data_source: Speech and language therapy reassessment notes, dietary chart, MDT stroke round notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic weekly speech and language therapy reassessment task to the stroke unit's electronic caseload for any patient on a modified diet, visible on the unit's therapy whiteboard until discontinued.
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT and speech and language therapy team meetings; embed the automatic weekly task permanently if reassessment rates improve.
pitfalls: Patients transferred to a rehabilitation ward may lose continuity of speech and language therapy follow-up → include a handover trigger for modified-diet patients on transfer
Staff shortages can deprioritise reassessment in favour of new patient screening → protect reassessment capacity as a distinct caseload category
'Stable' is not clearly defined, so reassessment may stop prematurely → agree a working definition (for example, no diet change for 2 consecutive reviews) before cycle 1
Weekly reassessment may be recorded informally without a clear date → use a structured, dated reassessment note
Long lengths of stay create a large caseload that can overwhelm capacity → monitor caseload size alongside compliance to identify staffing gaps
pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing dietary chart as a simple prompt for when reassessment is due
Agree a shared definition of 'stable' with the speech and language therapy team before starting data collection
Present caseload numbers alongside compliance rates to support any staffing business case that follows the audit
Track diet upgrades as a positive outcome measure, showing the reassessment process is clinically meaningful, not just procedural
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from speech and language therapy caseload records

question: What proportion of people with head and neck cancer having radiotherapy are offered a swallowing-exercise programme?
why: Radiotherapy to the head and neck causes progressive swallowing muscle stiffness, and pre-emptive exercise programmes can reduce long-term dysphagia, but referral is easily missed when speech and language therapy input is not built into the radiotherapy pathway. No audit of swallowing-exercise programme offer rates for head and neck radiotherapy patients has been published in the library; pre-treatment enteral nutrition assessment for this population has been audited separately [NNA-033].

standard.source: NICE NG36 Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management, recommendation 1.8.3 (2016)
standard.wording: Consider swallowing-exercise programmes for people having radiotherapy.

pass: Documented offer of a swallowing-exercise programme by speech and language therapy, made before or at the start of radiotherapy
population: Inclusion: adults with head and neck cancer starting radical or adjuvant radiotherapy. Exclusion: patients having palliative radiotherapy only, patients with pre-existing total laryngectomy
sample: 30-40 consecutive patients starting head and neck radiotherapy over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Head and neck MDT outcome form, speech and language therapy referral and assessment records, oncology treatment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'pre-radiotherapy swallowing exercise programme offered: yes/no' field to the head and neck MDT outcome form, completed by the MDT speech and language therapist before the radiotherapy planning appointment.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the head and neck cancer MDT meeting; embed the mandatory MDT form field permanently if offer rates improve.
evidence: [NNA-033] enteral nutrition need assessed at head and neck cancer diagnosis: audits nutrition assessment, not the swallowing-exercise programme audited here
pitfalls: Referral may happen but the exercise programme itself may not start before treatment begins → audit programme start date against radiotherapy start date, not referral alone
Patients may decline the programme due to treatment burden → record declines separately from the service failing to offer it
Speech and language therapy capacity in oncology services may be limited → identify capacity gaps as part of the audit's pitfalls, not just documentation gaps
MDT outcome forms may not have a dedicated field, making the offer hard to trace retrospectively → create the field before, not after, data collection begins
Patients treated at a different centre for radiotherapy may fall outside local documentation → clarify pathway responsibility for shared-care patients
pearls: Work with the head and neck cancer nurse specialist to identify the patient cohort quickly from MDT records
Time the swallowing-exercise programme offer to coincide with the pre-treatment dental and nutrition assessments already built into the pathway
Present long-term dysphagia outcome data alongside offer rates to strengthen the case for embedding the change
Keep a simple patient information leaflet ready so the offer can be made and accepted at the same appointment
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT and speech and language therapy records

question: What proportion of people with head and neck cancer whose voice has changed because of treatment are offered voice therapy?
why: Voice changes after surgery or radiotherapy for head and neck cancer have a major impact on quality of life and return to work, but voice therapy referral depends on the change being actively asked about and recorded at follow-up. No audit of voice therapy offer rates for treatment-related voice change has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG36 Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management, recommendation 1.8.5 (2016)
standard.wording: Consider voice therapy for people whose voice has changed because of their treatment.

pass: Documented assessment of voice change at the post-treatment follow-up appointment, with voice therapy offered when a change is identified
population: Inclusion: adults treated surgically or with radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, attending their first post-treatment follow-up appointment. Exclusion: patients with total laryngectomy already under voice rehabilitation, patients with recurrent disease requiring further treatment before follow-up
sample: 30-40 consecutive patients at their first post-treatment follow-up over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Oncology and ENT follow-up clinic letters, speech and language therapy referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'voice change: yes/no, therapy offered' field to the post-treatment follow-up clinic letter template, with a direct speech and language therapy referral link.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the head and neck cancer MDT and follow-up clinic governance meeting; embed the mandatory field permanently if offer rates improve.
pitfalls: Voice change may not be actively asked about unless prompted → use a direct question in the follow-up template rather than relying on the patient to raise it
Patients may not recognise a gradual voice change as treatment-related → provide a simple patient-facing prompt or questionnaire before the appointment
Voice therapy referral pathways may differ between ENT and oncology-led follow-up → clarify a single referral route before cycle 1
Some voice change may be expected and temporary, leading staff to under-refer → offer therapy for persistent change beyond an agreed time point (for example, 3 months)
Low clinic time may limit thorough voice assessment → consider a brief validated voice-related quality-of-life screening tool
pearls: Use a short, validated voice-related quality-of-life question set to standardise assessment across clinicians
Involve the ENT and oncology follow-up clinic teams jointly, since patients may attend either
Track referral-to-first-appointment time for voice therapy as a secondary outcome
Keep the referral link in the clinic letter template so it survives staff rotation
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from follow-up clinic records

question: What proportion of patients with communication difficulties suspected after stroke are referred to a speech and language therapist for detailed assessment?
why: Suspected communication difficulties identified by nursing or medical staff on the ward do not always translate into a formal speech and language therapy referral, particularly for patients with mild or fluctuating symptoms. No audit of referral completion for suspected post-stroke communication difficulties has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.3 (2013)
standard.wording: Refer people with suspected communication difficulties after stroke to a speech and language therapist for detailed analysis of any impairments and assessment of their impact.

pass: A documented speech and language therapy referral made within 24 hours of a suspected communication difficulty being recorded
population: Inclusion: adults after stroke with a documented suspicion of a communication difficulty (from screening or ward observation). Exclusion: patients already known to have a pre-existing communication impairment unrelated to the stroke
sample: 40 consecutive stroke patients with a documented suspected communication difficulty over the last 3 months
data_source: Nursing and medical notes, communication screening results, speech and language therapy referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Link the stroke unit's communication screening tool directly to an automatic speech and language therapy referral in the EPR whenever a suspected difficulty is recorded, removing the need for a separate manual referral step.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT meeting; embed the automatic referral link permanently if compliance improves.
pitfalls: A suspicion noted informally in ward round notes may not be recognised as needing referral → tie referral directly to the structured screening tool result, not free-text impressions
Weekend suspicion may wait until Monday for referral → report weekday/weekend referral timing separately
Referral may be made but the detailed assessment delayed by caseload pressure → audit both referral and completed assessment as separate steps
Mild or fluctuating symptoms may be under-recognised by non-specialist staff → provide brief training on recognising subtle communication difficulties
Duplicate referrals from multiple staff members may distort the true referral rate → count time-to-first-referral, not total referrals
pearls: Build the automatic referral into the same screening tool used for the 72-hour communication screening audit
Agree an escalation route for referrals not actioned within 24 hours with the speech and language therapy team lead
Report referral-to-assessment interval as well as referral rate to show the whole pathway working
Use ward-based posters or prompts to help non-specialist staff recognise subtle communication difficulties
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from ward and referral records

question: What proportion of stroke patients with severe communication difficulties are assessed by a speech and language therapist for their potential to benefit from a communication aid or technology?
why: Communication aids can restore a degree of independence and participation for people with severe aphasia or dysarthria, but assessment for aids is easily overlooked once initial rehabilitation therapy is under way. No audit of communication aid assessment completion for stroke patients with severe communication difficulties has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.7 (2013)
standard.wording: Speech and language therapists should assess people experiencing severe communication difficulties after stroke to see if they could benefit from using a communication aid or other technologies (for example, home-based computer therapies or mobile apps).

pass: A documented speech and language therapy assessment for communication aid or technology suitability, completed within 4 weeks of a severe communication difficulty being confirmed
population: Inclusion: adults after stroke with a speech and language therapy diagnosis of severe aphasia or dysarthria. Exclusion: patients who die or are discharged to end-of-life care before assessment could reasonably occur
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Speech and language therapy assessment and treatment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'communication aid assessment due' flag to the speech and language therapy caseload system for any patient coded with severe aphasia or dysarthria, reviewed weekly at the therapy team meeting.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the speech and language therapy and stroke MDT meetings; embed the caseload flag permanently if assessment rates improve.
pitfalls: Severity of aphasia or dysarthria may not be consistently graded, making the eligible population hard to define → agree a clear severity threshold or tool before cycle 1
Assessment may be deprioritised in favour of more immediate rehabilitation goals → build a caseload flag so it is not forgotten, not competing informally for attention
Aids assessed as suitable may not be provided promptly due to funding or equipment delays → audit provision as well as assessment
Patients discharged to community speech and language therapy may lose continuity → include a handover field confirming the assessment need is passed on
Family or carer engagement is often needed for technology use, and its absence can be mistaken for the patient's inability to benefit → record carer involvement separately
pearls: Agree a shared definition of 'severe' communication difficulty with the whole speech and language therapy team before starting
Use the caseload flag system already in place for other therapy follow-up tasks rather than creating a new one
