Track aid uptake and use at follow-up, not just assessment completion, to show the change is meaningful
Involve community speech and language therapy early so continuity is maintained after hospital discharge
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from speech and language therapy caseload records

question: What proportion of stroke patients with dysphagia who cannot, or find it difficult to, follow a mouth care regimen have a suitably trained healthcare professional, family member or carer delivering or supervising their mouth care?
why: Poor oral hygiene in dysphagia increases the risk of aspiration pneumonia, but mouth care is often left to whichever staff member is available rather than someone trained and briefed by speech and language therapy. No audit of supervised mouth care provision for stroke patients with dysphagia has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.10.3 (2023)
standard.wording: Ensure that a suitably trained healthcare professional, family member or carer delivers or supervises mouth care for people after stroke who cannot, or find it difficult to, follow a mouth care regimen.

pass: Documented mouth care delivered or supervised at least twice daily by a named trained healthcare professional, family member or carer, for a patient with dysphagia unable to independently follow a mouth care regimen
population: Inclusion: adults after stroke with dysphagia and a documented difficulty following a mouth care regimen independently. Exclusion: patients independent with mouth care, patients receiving end-of-life comfort care with a separate mouth care plan
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3 months
data_source: Nursing mouth care charts, speech and language therapy dysphagia management plan
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a structured mouth care chart to the dysphagia management plan, naming the trained staff member or family/carer responsible for each shift, with speech and language therapy providing brief training as part of the initial dysphagia assessment.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the stroke MDT and tissue viability/infection prevention meetings, given the aspiration pneumonia link; embed the structured mouth care chart permanently if compliance improves.
pitfalls: Mouth care is often delegated informally without checking staff training → build a simple training checklist into ward induction for stroke unit staff
Family involvement can be inconsistent if visiting hours are limited → record attempts to involve family separately from successful involvement
Mouth care charts may exist but not be completed consistently → use a structured chart requiring a signature at each episode
Patients who resist mouth care because of reduced consciousness or agitation are miscounted as failures → record refusals and adapted approaches as a distinct category
Aspiration pneumonia rates may have multiple causes, complicating outcome attribution → present mouth care compliance as a process measure alongside, not instead of, pneumonia rates
pearls: Ask speech and language therapy to provide a short, standard mouth care training session for ward staff as part of stroke unit induction
Use a simple laminated mouth care chart at the bedside rather than relying on the general nursing care plan
Track aspiration pneumonia rates over the audit period as a secondary outcome to strengthen the clinical case
Involve family members proactively by giving them a simple mouth care information leaflet on admission
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from nursing mouth care charts

question: What proportion of adult inpatients are screened for the risk of malnutrition using a validated screening tool within 24 hours of admission?
why: Malnutrition on admission is common and worsens outcomes, but screening can be delayed or skipped entirely on busy admission wards. No closed-loop audit of the timeliness of malnutrition screening on admission (as opposed to weekly re-screening for a single surgical specialty) has been published in the library; weekly re-screening for hip fracture inpatients has been audited separately [ONA-007], and documentation of a care plan after a high MUST score has been audited separately [NNA-274].

standard.source: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 1 (2012)
standard.wording: All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and for outpatients if there is clinical concern.

pass: A documented MUST (or other validated tool) screening score completed within 24 hours of hospital admission
population: Inclusion: all adults admitted as an emergency or elective inpatient. Exclusion: patients who die or are discharged within 24 hours of admission, patients admitted for less than an overnight stay
sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions across 2-3 general medical and surgical wards over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Nursing admission assessment, MUST screening tool documentation in the EPR
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make MUST screening a mandatory field in the electronic nursing admission assessment that cannot be saved as complete until entered, with an overdue alert visible on the ward safety board after 24 hours.
reaudit: 8-10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition steering group and ward safety huddles; embed the mandatory EPR field permanently if screening rates improve.
evidence: [ONA-007] weekly MUST re-screening for hip fracture inpatients, [NNA-274] nutrition care plan documented within 48 hours of a high MUST score: audit later steps in the nutrition pathway, not initial screening timeliness across general admissions
pitfalls: Screening may be attempted but not fully completed (for example, weight recorded but height missing) → count only fully completed, scoreable screens as a pass

Patients unable to be weighed (bed-bound, confused) may be recorded as 'not screened' when an alternative method should be used → record use of alternative MUST methods (ulna length, mid-upper arm circumference) as a valid pass
Night admissions may be screened just after the 24-hour window due to shift patterns → report the distribution of screening times, not just a pass/fail cut-off
Screening completed but not scored or acted on undermines the purpose → pair this audit with monitoring of action taken on high-risk scores
Improvement may not be sustained without an EPR hard stop → avoid relying on a paper reminder alone
pearls: Use the trust's existing MUST screening field in the EPR rather than creating a new one
Recruit ward-based nutrition link nurses to champion the mandatory field change
Present results by ward and by day of week to identify where gaps cluster
Feed screening completion rates into the same dashboard used for other admission-bundle metrics so it becomes part of routine ward governance
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from admission records

question: What proportion of adult inpatients with a MUST score indicating high risk have a dietitian referral, or another defined local nutrition action, made on the same day as the screen?
why: Identifying high malnutrition risk has no benefit unless it triggers timely action, but referral can be delayed while a patient waits for a ward round or is missed altogether. No audit of same-day action following a high-risk MUST score has been published in the library; documentation of a nutrition care plan within 48 hours has been audited separately [NNA-274].

standard.source: BAPEN MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool)
standard.wording: Refer to dietitian, Nutritional Support Team or implement local policy. Set goals, improve and increase overall nutritional intake. Monitor and review care plan.

pass: A documented dietitian referral or defined local nutrition action taken on the same day as a MUST score of 2 or more is recorded
population: Inclusion: adult inpatients with a MUST score of 2 or more. Exclusion: patients already under active dietetic review for another reason at the time of screening, patients receiving end-of-life comfort care only
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a MUST score of 2 or more over the last 2-3 months
data_source: MUST screening record, dietitian referral log, nursing care plan
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the EPR to automatically generate a dietitian referral and pre-populate a basic local nutrition action plan whenever a MUST score of 2 or more is entered.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition steering group meeting; embed the automatic referral trigger permanently if same-day action rates improve.
evidence: [NNA-274] nutrition care plan documented within 48 hours of a high MUST score: audits documentation completeness at 48 hours rather than whether action is taken on the same day as screening
pitfalls: High-scoring patients may be seen by the dietitian eventually but not on the same day → record the exact interval, not just whether action ever happened
Weekend screening may have no same-day dietetic cover → report weekday versus weekend rates separately and consider a nursing-led interim action for weekends
Some wards may have an informal local policy (for example, fortified diet menu) that is not documented as a formal action → make 'local policy action' an explicit, codeable option
Automatic referrals may generate an unmanageable volume for the dietetic service → monitor referral volume and dietetic capacity alongside compliance
Duplicate referrals for patients already known to dietetics may inflate apparent non-compliance → exclude patients already under active review
pearls: Agree the same-day interim nursing action (for example, starting food record charts and fortified diet) with dietetics before the automatic referral is built
Use the existing MUST screening EPR field as the trigger point rather than creating a parallel system
Track dietetic referral volume weekly during the pilot to catch capacity problems early
Report same-day action rates to ward sisters as well as dietetics, since nursing staff often make the first move
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from screening and referral records

question: What proportion of adults identified as high risk of refeeding syndrome have nutrition support introduced at no more than 50% of their estimated requirements for the first 2 days?
why: Starting nutrition support too quickly in patients at high risk of refeeding syndrome can precipitate dangerous electrolyte shifts and cardiac complications, but the cautious starting rate is easy to overlook when a patient appears simply malnourished rather than acutely at risk. No audit of the initial feeding rate for high-refeeding-risk patients has been published in the library; thiamine provision before feeding starts has been audited separately [NNA-382].

standard.source: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults, recommendation 1.4.5 (2006)
standard.wording: People who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support introduced at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, before increasing feed rates to meet full needs if clinical and biochemical monitoring reveals no refeeding problems.

pass: Documented nutrition support prescription at no more than 50% of estimated requirements for the first 2 days in a patient meeting the high-refeeding-risk criteria, with biochemical monitoring recorded
population: Inclusion: adults starting enteral or parenteral nutrition support who meet the high-risk refeeding criteria (for example, little or no intake for more than 5 days, or the CG32 box 1 criteria). Exclusion: patients started on nutrition support in a critical care setting with a separate unit-specific protocol
sample: 30-40 consecutive high-refeeding-risk patients starting nutrition support over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Dietetic assessment and feeding plan, nutrition prescription chart, biochemistry results
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory refeeding risk box to the enteral and parenteral nutrition prescription form that, when ticked, pre-sets the feed rate to no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days and prompts daily biochemical monitoring.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition support team and pharmacy governance meeting; embed the prescription form default permanently if compliance improves.
evidence: [NNA-382] thiamine given before tube feeding or parenteral nutrition in high refeeding risk: audits a related but distinct element of the same CG32 refeeding pathway
pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be systematically checked before feeding starts → build a structured criteria checklist into the dietetic assessment
Estimated requirements may be calculated inconsistently between staff → use a standard calculation method agreed with dietetics
Out-of-hours feeding may start before dietetic review, at full rate by default → provide a simple out-of-hours prescribing guide for medical and nursing staff
Biochemical monitoring may be requested but results not reviewed promptly → audit both request and same-day review of results
Feed rate may be recorded on a nursing chart but not cross-checked against the prescription → use one shared, agreed feeding rate record
pearls: Provide a quick-reference refeeding risk card for out-of-hours medical staff, since risk is often first identified outside normal dietetic hours
Agree the standard requirement calculation and prescribing defaults with the nutrition support team and pharmacy together
Track biochemical abnormalities and complications as a secondary outcome to demonstrate the safety benefit of compliance
Keep a small dietetic on-call or telephone advice service, where feasible, to support out-of-hours refeeding decisions
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from dietetic and prescribing records

question: What proportion of adults screened for malnutrition risk have their screening result and any nutrition support goals documented and communicated in writing within and between care settings?
why: A completed malnutrition screen is of little value if the result and any nutrition support plan are not passed on when a patient moves ward, is transferred, or is discharged, risking nutrition support stopping unexpectedly. No audit of written communication of nutrition screening results between settings has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 3 (2012)
standard.wording: All people who are screened for the risk of malnutrition have their screening results and nutrition support goals (if applicable), documented and communicated in writing within and between settings.

pass: The most recent MUST score and any nutrition support goals are documented in the discharge summary or transfer letter for a patient moving between wards, hospitals, or to community/primary care
population: Inclusion: adults with a documented MUST screen who are discharged or transferred during the audit period. Exclusion: patients who die as an inpatient, patients transferred to another department within the same ward round without a formal handover document
sample: 40 consecutive discharges or transfers with a prior MUST screen over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Discharge summary, transfer letter, MUST screening record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'most recent MUST score and nutrition support goals' field to the electronic discharge summary and transfer letter templates, auto-populated from the current MUST record.
reaudit: 10 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition steering group and discharge planning governance meeting; embed the auto-populated field permanently if communication rates improve.
pitfalls: Screening results may be documented in the EPR but not carried into the discharge letter, which is what primary care and care homes actually see → audit the discharge letter specifically, not the EPR record alone
Nutrition goals may be informal (for example, verbal advice) and not written down → require a structured goals field, not free text alone
Auto-population may fail if the discharge letter is generated before the final MUST score is entered → sequence the discharge workflow so nutrition data is finalised first
Community and care home recipients may not act on the information even when it is communicated → consider tracking whether GP or care home nutrition action follows, as a stretch outcome
High volume of standard discharge letters may make manual auditing slow → use a coded search for the mandatory field once implemented
pearls: Work with the IT/EPR team to auto-populate the discharge letter from the existing MUST record rather than requiring manual entry
Include this as a checklist item in the trust's standard discharge safety checklist
Present results alongside readmission data, since unclear nutrition handover is a recognised contributor to early readmission
Share results with community dietetics and care home liaison teams, who are the ultimate recipients of this information
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from discharge documentation

question: What proportion of new outpatients are screened for the risk of malnutrition using a validated tool at their first clinic appointment?
why: Malnutrition screening is well established for hospital inpatients but far less consistently applied in outpatient clinics, where at-risk patients (for example, with cancer, gastrointestinal or respiratory disease) can go unidentified for months. No audit of first-appointment outpatient malnutrition screening has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 1 (2012)
standard.wording: All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and for outpatients if there is clinical concern.

pass: A documented MUST or other validated malnutrition screening score recorded at the patient's first attendance at the clinic
population: Inclusion: adults attending their first appointment at a named outpatient clinic (for example, gastroenterology, oncology, respiratory). Exclusion: follow-up appointments, telephone or video-only consultations where weight cannot be obtained
sample: 40 consecutive new outpatient attendances at 1-2 clinics over the last 2-3 months
data_source: Outpatient clinic letter, nursing pre-clinic assessment, EPR screening field
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a MUST screening step (weight, height or alternative measure, and unintentional weight loss question) to the pre-clinic nursing check-in for new outpatient appointments in the selected specialties, feeding directly into the clinic letter.
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the specialty clinic governance meeting and nutrition steering group; embed the pre-clinic screening step permanently if uptake improves.
pitfalls: Outpatient clinics often lack scales or a private space to weigh patients → confirm basic equipment is available before cycle 1
Nursing or clinic support staff capacity to add a new screening step may be limited → pilot in 1-2 high-yield clinics first, not trust-wide
Patients attending by telephone or video cannot be physically screened → exclude these from the denominator or use a self-reported alternative
A positive screen may not lead to a dietitian referral if no clear pathway exists in outpatients → agree the outpatient referral route before starting data collection
Clinics with high patient turnover may see screening as adding unacceptable time → use the shortest validated tool and involve clinic staff in timing it before rollout
pearls: Start with a clinic where malnutrition risk is clinically plausible and staff are receptive (for example, oncology or gastroenterology) to build a strong case study
Provide a simple self-completion weight-loss question card that patients can fill in the waiting room to save clinic time
Agree the outpatient dietitian referral pathway with the dietetic service before starting, so a positive screen has somewhere to go
Report time-per-patient added by screening, to reassure clinic managers ahead of wider rollout
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic and screening records

question: What proportion of adults at high risk of refeeding problems are cared for by staff with documented expert knowledge of nutritional requirements and nutrition support?
why: Managing high refeeding risk safely requires specific expertise in fluid, electrolyte and micronutrient management, but out-of-hours or general ward staff without this training sometimes manage these patients without specialist input. No audit of whether high-refeeding-risk patients are cared for by appropriately trained staff has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults, recommendation 1.4.7 (2006)
standard.wording: People at high risk of developing refeeding problems (box 1) should be cared for by healthcare professionals who are appropriately skilled and trained and have expert knowledge of nutritional requirements and nutrition support.

pass: Documented dietitian or nutrition support team involvement in the care of a high-refeeding-risk patient from the point of identification until they are stable
population: Inclusion: adults meeting the high-risk refeeding criteria (CG32 box 1) starting nutrition support. Exclusion: patients managed in a critical care unit with a dedicated intensivist-led nutrition protocol
sample: 30-40 consecutive high-risk patients over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Dietetic referral and review notes, nutrition support team involvement records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic same-day dietitian and nutrition support team referral trigger to the EPR whenever high refeeding risk criteria are documented, with a weekend on-call dietetic advice line for urgent queries.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition support team governance meeting; embed the automatic referral trigger and on-call advice line permanently if compliance improves.
pitfalls: High risk may be identified out of hours when specialist dietetic cover is unavailable → provide a documented on-call or telephone advice route
General ward staff may feel confident managing 'mild' malnutrition without recognising true refeeding risk → provide brief training on the box 1 high-risk criteria
Specialist involvement may be a single initial review without ongoing follow-up until stability → audit ongoing review, not just the first contact
Locum or rotating junior medical staff may be unfamiliar with the referral pathway → include it in induction materials
Nutrition support team capacity may be limited, especially out of hours → monitor referral volume and capacity as part of the fix, not just compliance
pearls: Provide a simple laminated card of the box 1 high-risk criteria for admission areas and out-of-hours teams
Agree an on-call dietetic advice arrangement (even a telephone rota) before rolling out the automatic referral trigger
Track biochemical complications as a secondary outcome to show the safety value of specialist involvement
Include the referral pathway in trust induction for new medical and nursing staff so knowledge does not depend on individual experience
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from dietetic and nutrition support team records

question: What proportion of patients receiving complex enteral or parenteral nutrition support are reviewed by the multidisciplinary nutrition support team?
why: Complex nutrition support, particularly parenteral nutrition, carries risks that are best managed with input from doctors, dietitians, specialist nurses and pharmacists working together, but individual disciplines can end up managing these patients in parallel rather than through the team. No audit of multidisciplinary nutrition support team review completion has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults (2006)
standard.wording: All acute hospital trusts should have a multidisciplinary nutrition support team, which may include: doctors...dietitians, a specialist nutrition nurse, other nurses, pharmacists, biochemistry and microbiology laboratory support staff, and other allied healthcare professionals.

pass: Documented review by the multidisciplinary nutrition support team (or, where a formal team does not exist, joint documented input from a dietitian, doctor and pharmacist) within 3 working days of starting parenteral nutrition or complex enteral feeding
population: Inclusion: adults starting parenteral nutrition, or enteral feeding via a surgically placed tube, or feeding expected to continue for more than 4 weeks. Exclusion: patients on short-term nasogastric feeding expected to last less than 2 weeks
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Nutrition support team referral and review documentation, prescribing records for parenteral nutrition
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set an automatic nutrition support team referral whenever parenteral nutrition or a complex enteral feeding tube is prescribed, with a standing weekly nutrition support team ward round to review all open referrals.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the nutrition support team and pharmacy governance meeting; embed the automatic referral and standing ward round permanently if review rates improve.
pitfalls: Some trusts may not have a formally constituted nutrition support team, making 'review' hard to define → agree a minimum joint-input definition (dietitian, doctor, pharmacist) before starting where no formal team exists
Parenteral nutrition may be started out of hours before the team can review → audit the interval to first review, not same-day review alone
Referral may happen without a documented outcome → require a written review note, not just a referral entry
Complex feeding started on a surgical ward may not be flagged to the nutrition support team if ownership is unclear → clarify referral responsibility with surgical teams before cycle 1
Capacity of the nutrition support team may limit how many reviews can happen within 3 working days → monitor team capacity alongside compliance
pearls: Use parenteral nutrition prescribing records as the simplest way to identify the sample
Agree the automatic referral trigger with pharmacy, since parenteral nutrition prescriptions usually pass through pharmacy first
Present line-related and metabolic complication rates alongside review compliance to show the clinical value of the change
Keep the weekly nutrition support team ward round visible on the hospital's clinical governance calendar so it does not quietly lapse
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from nutrition support team records

question: What proportion of patients discharged home on enteral tube feeding have a coordinated community multidisciplinary follow-up plan, including a named dietitian, GP and district nursing contact, arranged before discharge?
why: Enteral tube feeding at home depends on a well-coordinated community team, but discharge planning can focus on the equipment and miss arranging the ongoing multidisciplinary follow-up itself, risking feeding interruptions or unrecognised complications after discharge. No audit of community multidisciplinary follow-up arrangements for home enteral tube feeding has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults (2006)
standard.wording: All people in the community having enteral tube feeding should be supported by a coordinated multidisciplinary team, which includes dietitians, district, care home or homecare company nurses, GPs, community pharmacists and other allied healthcare professionals... Close liaison between the multidisciplinary team and patients and carers regarding diagnoses, prescription, arrangements and potential problems is essential.

pass: A documented discharge plan naming a community dietitian, GP and district/homecare nursing contact for ongoing enteral feeding support, completed before the patient leaves hospital
population: Inclusion: adults discharged home or to a care home on enteral tube feeding. Exclusion: patients discharged to another acute hospital or hospice, patients whose tube feeding is expected to stop before discharge
sample: 30-40 consecutive patients discharged on home enteral tube feeding over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Discharge summary, dietetic discharge planning notes, community referral forms
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory home enteral feeding discharge checklist to the EPR, requiring named community dietitian, GP and district/homecare nursing contacts before the discharge summary can be finalised.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the dietetics and discharge planning governance meeting; embed the mandatory checklist permanently if completion rates improve.
pitfalls: Community dietetic and homecare services may vary in how referrals are received, causing delays → map the local referral routes before cycle 1
Discharge may be expedited under bed pressure before all community contacts are confirmed → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge summary
GP notification may happen via a generic discharge letter without a specific enteral feeding flag → add an explicit enteral feeding section to the discharge letter template
Care home residents may have different notification pathways than those discharged to their own home → record discharge destination and adapt accordingly
Patients or carers may not retain the contact details given → provide a printed, single-page 'who to contact' card in addition to the discharge letter
pearls: Work with the homecare feeding company (where one is used) to build a standard discharge checklist together
Involve the community dietetic service in designing the checklist so referrals arrive in the format they need
Give patients and carers a simple laminated contact card, not just a paragraph buried in a longer discharge letter
Track unplanned readmissions related to feeding problems as a secondary outcome to show the value of coordinated discharge
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from discharge and dietetic records

question: What proportion of adults with diabetes and a new active (non-limb-threatening) foot problem are referred to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service within 1 working day, with triage completed within 1 further working day?
why: Active diabetic foot problems can progress rapidly to limb-threatening infection or ulceration if referral is delayed, but referral timing outside the inpatient setting (for example, from primary care, podiatry clinics or the emergency department) is rarely tracked. No audit of the 1-working-day referral and triage standard for new active diabetic foot problems has been published in the library; inpatient admission foot examination timing has been audited separately [ONA-078, NNA-114].

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.4.2 (2015)
standard.wording: For all other active diabetic foot problems, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service (according to local protocols and pathways...) for triage within 1 further working day.

pass: Documented referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service within 1 working day of a new active (non-limb-threatening) diabetic foot problem being identified, with triage recorded within 1 further working day
population: Inclusion: adults with diabetes presenting with a new active foot problem (ulceration, infection, or suspected Charcot arthropathy) that is not immediately limb- or life-threatening, identified in primary care, community podiatry, the emergency department or outpatient clinics. Exclusion: limb- or life-threatening presentations requiring immediate acute referral, patients already under active multidisciplinary foot care service follow-up
sample: 30-40 consecutive new active diabetic foot problems identified over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Podiatry, GP and emergency department referral records, multidisciplinary foot care service triage log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a single, well-publicised electronic referral route (fax-free, one form) to the multidisciplinary foot care service accessible from primary care, community podiatry and the emergency department, with a same-day triage response built into the podiatry team's daily workflow.
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team and primary care network meeting; embed the single referral route permanently if timeliness improves.
evidence: [ONA-078] diabetic foot examination within 24 hours of orthopaedic admission, [NNA-114] diabetic foot risk assessment within 24 hours of medical admission: audit inpatient admission foot examination, not referral and triage timing for new active problems identified outside the inpatient admission pathway
pitfalls: Referrers outside the acute trust (GPs, community podiatrists) may not know the correct referral route → publicise a single, simple referral pathway across primary and community care
Weekend or bank holiday presentations may miss the 1-working-day target through no fault of the referrer → report working-day compliance rather than calendar-day compliance
Referral date may be recorded as the date the letter is typed rather than the date the problem was identified → clarify the start point as clinical identification, not paperwork
Triage delay may occur even when referral is prompt, if the foot service is under-resourced → audit referral and triage timeliness as separate steps
Different definitions of 'active' foot problem may be applied inconsistently → use the NG19 risk stratification definitions explicitly in the audit template
pearls: Agree a single, shared referral form and route with primary care, the emergency department and community podiatry before starting data collection
Recruit a podiatry team lead and a GP with an interest in diabetes as joint audit leads to bridge primary and secondary care
Track referral source to identify where delays cluster and target the fix accordingly
Report results to the local diabetes network, not just the acute trust, since most referrals originate outside hospital
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from referral and triage records

question: What proportion of adults with diabetes have their risk of developing a foot problem formally assessed at diagnosis and at least annually thereafter?
why: Annual diabetic foot risk assessment identifies people who need referral to podiatry before problems develop, but recall systems can lapse, particularly for patients who do not attend routine diabetes reviews. No audit of the annual foot risk assessment standard itself (as distinct from inpatient admission foot checks) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.3 (2015)
standard.wording: For adults with diabetes, assess their risk of developing a diabetic foot problem at the following times: When diabetes is diagnosed, and at least annually thereafter...

pass: A documented foot risk assessment (both feet examined, risk stratified as low, moderate, high or active) recorded within the last 12 months for a patient with an established diagnosis of diabetes
population: Inclusion: adults with a diabetes diagnosis of 12 months or more registered with the practice or diabetes service. Exclusion: patients who have had a bilateral lower limb amputation, patients who declined the assessment despite being offered it
sample: 40 consecutive adults with diabetes due an annual review over the last 3 months
data_source: GP or diabetes clinic annual review template, podiatry/foot risk assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automated 12-monthly recall to the practice or diabetes service's electronic register that flags any patient overdue a foot risk assessment, generating a reminder letter or text message.
reaudit: 3-4 months later (allowing time for recalls to take effect), same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetes network and primary care network meeting; embed the automated recall permanently if assessment rates improve.
pitfalls: Patients who do not attend routine diabetes reviews are systematically missed → track non-attendance rates and consider opportunistic assessment at any contact
Foot risk assessment may be recorded without formal risk stratification, making the record hard to audit → require the risk category as a discrete, codeable field
Care home residents or housebound patients may be excluded from clinic-based recall systems → arrange domiciliary foot assessment as an alternative pathway
Multiple providers (GP, diabetes clinic, podiatry) may each believe the other completed the assessment → agree a single named responsible service
A high proportion of 'not recorded' risk categories can mask assessments that were actually done but poorly documented → review free-text notes as well as coded fields where discrepancies arise
pearls: Use the practice's existing diabetes register and recall system rather than building a new one from scratch
Agree a single coded risk-category field with the clinical system supplier so the data is auditable going forward
Prioritise recall for patients not seen in the last 15 months to catch those falling furthest behind
Report results back to individual GP practices within the network to drive local ownership
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from GP and diabetes clinic records

question: What proportion of adults newly referred to the foot protection service are assessed within the recommended timeframe for their risk category: 2 to 4 weeks for high risk and 6 to 8 weeks for moderate risk?
why: Foot protection service waiting times directly affect whether a moderate- or high-risk foot is assessed before it deteriorates, but waiting list pressures can push assessment beyond the recommended window without this being routinely tracked. No audit of foot protection service assessment timeliness by risk category has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.9 (2015)
standard.wording: The foot protection service should assess newly referred people as follows: Within 2 to 4 weeks for people who are at high risk of developing a diabetic foot problem. Within 6 to 8 weeks for people who are at moderate risk of developing a diabetic foot problem.

pass: First foot protection service assessment completed within 4 weeks of referral for high-risk patients, or within 8 weeks for moderate-risk patients
population: Inclusion: adults newly referred to the foot protection service with a stated risk category of moderate or high. Exclusion: patients referred with an active or limb-threatening foot problem (managed via a different, faster pathway)
sample: 40 consecutive new foot protection service referrals over the last 3-4 months
data_source: Podiatry referral and appointment booking system
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce risk-stratified booking slots in the podiatry appointment system, so high-risk referrals are automatically offered an appointment within 4 weeks and moderate-risk referrals within 8 weeks, with a waiting list review meeting if targets are at risk of being breached.
target: ≥85% of referrals meeting the timeframe for their risk category
reaudit: 12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the podiatry service governance and diabetes network meeting; embed risk-stratified booking permanently if waiting times improve.
pitfalls: Risk category may not be clearly stated on the referral, defaulting patients to a lower-priority slot → make risk category a mandatory referral field
Capacity constraints may mean the whole service is over target, not just poorly prioritised → report absolute waiting times alongside risk-stratified compliance to distinguish the two problems
Patients may cancel or rearrange their first appointment, extending the apparent wait → record patient-caused delays separately from service delays
Referrals from different sources (GP, hospital, self-referral) may use inconsistent risk terminology → provide a simple risk-category reference for all referrers
Improvement gained by re-prioritising existing capacity may simply shift delays to lower-risk patients → monitor low-risk waiting times too, to avoid an unintended consequence
pearls: Use the podiatry booking system's existing data fields to build the risk-stratified reporting rather than a manual log
Share risk-category definitions with all major referrers (GP practices, diabetes clinics, hospital wards) before making risk category mandatory
Present waiting time data by risk category monthly to the podiatry team so slippage is caught early, not only at re-audit
Use the audit to support any business case for additional podiatry capacity if absolute waiting times, not just prioritisation, are the underlying problem
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the podiatry booking system

question: What proportion of adults known to the foot protection service are reassessed at the interval appropriate to their risk category (annually for low risk, every 3-6 months for moderate risk, every 1-2 months for high risk)?
why: Ongoing surveillance intervals matter as much as the initial assessment, but recall systems can allow moderate- and high-risk patients to drift onto a less frequent review cycle than their risk warrants. No audit of ongoing reassessment interval compliance by diabetic foot risk category has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.11 (2015, updated 2023)
standard.wording: Depending on the person's risk of developing a diabetic foot problem, carry out reassessments at the following intervals: Annually for people who are at low risk, as part of their annual diabetes review. Frequently (for example, every 3 to 6 months) for people who are at moderate risk. More frequently (for example, every 1 to 2 months) for people who are at high risk, if there is no immediate concern.

pass: The interval between the two most recent foot risk reassessments is within the recommended range for the patient's documented risk category at the earlier assessment
population: Inclusion: adults with diabetes known to the foot protection service with a documented risk category of moderate or high, and at least two recorded assessments. Exclusion: patients discharged from the foot protection service, patients whose risk category changed to active (managed via the active foot pathway) between assessments
sample: 30-40 consecutive moderate- or high-risk patients with two recent assessments over the last 6 months
data_source: Podiatry/foot protection service assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automated recall reminder to the podiatry caseload system that flags patients approaching or exceeding their risk-appropriate reassessment interval, reviewed weekly by the administrative team.
reaudit: 3-4 months later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the podiatry service governance meeting; embed the automated recall reminder permanently if interval compliance improves.
pitfalls: Risk category can change between assessments, complicating which interval applies → use the risk category recorded at the earlier of the two assessments
Patients who miss or cancel appointments extend the interval through no fault of the service → record patient non-attendance separately from service delay
High-risk patients needing very frequent review (every 1-2 months) generate a large recall workload → ensure administrative capacity matches the recall volume before rollout
Recall systems may not distinguish moderate from high risk automatically → build risk category into the recall system as a discrete field, not a free-text note
Patients discharged and re-referred may show an artificially long interval → exclude re-referred patients or flag them separately
pearls: Build the recall system on the podiatry service's existing caseload database rather than a standalone spreadsheet
Agree recall administrative responsibility explicitly, since this task is easy to lose between clinical and administrative staff
Report interval compliance by risk category separately, since high-risk patients are most vulnerable to slippage
Use missed and rearranged appointment data to identify patients who may need a different reminder method (text message, phone call)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from podiatry caseload records

question: What proportion of hospital inpatients at moderate or high risk of a diabetic foot problem are given a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure, and referred or notified to the foot protection service on discharge?
why: Inpatients with diabetes at moderate or high foot risk are vulnerable to heel pressure damage during a hospital stay, and the transition to community foot care surveillance after discharge is easily missed if notification is not built into the discharge process. No audit of heel offloading device provision and discharge notification to the foot protection service has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.12 (2015)
standard.wording: People in hospital who are at moderate or high risk of developing a diabetic foot problem should be given a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure. On discharge they should be referred or notified to the foot protection service.

pass: Documented provision of a heel pressure redistribution device during the admission, and a documented referral or notification to the foot protection service recorded in the discharge summary
population: Inclusion: adults with diabetes admitted to hospital with a documented moderate or high diabetic foot risk category. Exclusion: patients with an active foot problem already under multidisciplinary foot care service follow-up, patients who die as an inpatient
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible inpatients over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Nursing pressure area care records, tissue viability equipment log, discharge summary
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'diabetic foot risk: moderate/high → heel offloading device provided, FPS notified on discharge' prompt to the diabetes inpatient nursing bundle and the electronic discharge summary template.
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the tissue viability and diabetes inpatient team meeting; embed the discharge summary prompt permanently if compliance improves.
pitfalls: Heel offloading devices may not be readily stocked on general wards → confirm equipment availability with tissue viability before cycle 1
Foot risk category may not be documented for inpatients unless specifically prompted → link this audit to any existing inpatient foot risk assessment process
Discharge summaries may mention diabetes generally without a specific foot protection service notification → require an explicit, separate field
Patients transferred between wards may lose their heel offloading device without it being reordered → include a ward-transfer equipment check
Notification to the foot protection service may happen verbally or informally and go unrecorded → require a written notification, ideally electronic
pearls: Combine this with any existing inpatient diabetic foot risk assessment audit to use the same case list
Work with tissue viability to ensure heel offloading equipment is readily available on wards with high numbers of diabetes admissions
Build the foot protection service notification into the same discharge workflow as other community referrals, rather than a separate process
Track heel pressure ulcer incidence in this population as a secondary outcome to demonstrate impact
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from nursing and discharge records

question: When diabetic foot ulcer debridement is carried out in hospital, is it done only by a healthcare professional from the multidisciplinary foot care service?
why: Debridement of diabetic foot ulcers by staff without specialist foot care training can damage healthy tissue or miss deeper infection, but ad hoc debridement by general surgical or ward staff can occur when the multidisciplinary foot care service is not readily available. No audit of who performs inpatient diabetic foot ulcer debridement has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.5.7 (2015)
standard.wording: When treating diabetic foot ulcers, debridement in hospital should only be done by healthcare professionals from the multidisciplinary foot care service, using the technique that best matches their specialist expertise and clinical experience, the site of the diabetic foot ulcer and the person's preference.

pass: Documented record that every debridement episode for a diabetic foot ulcer during the hospital stay was performed by a named member of the multidisciplinary foot care service
population: Inclusion: adults with diabetes admitted to hospital with a foot ulcer requiring debridement during the stay. Exclusion: debridement performed as part of a major surgical procedure (for example, formal surgical debridement under general anaesthetic led by the surgical team as part of an agreed multidisciplinary foot care service plan)
sample: 30 consecutive inpatient diabetic foot ulcer debridement episodes over the last 4-6 months
data_source: Wound care and podiatry treatment notes, theatre records where relevant
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'debridement performed by' field, restricted to named multidisciplinary foot care service staff, to the wound care documentation for diabetic foot ulcers, with an alert if a non-specialist attempts to document a debridement episode.
target: 100% of debridement episodes performed by multidisciplinary foot care service staff
reaudit: 10-12 weeks later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team and tissue viability governance meeting; embed the restricted documentation field permanently if compliance reaches target.
pitfalls: Ward nursing staff may perform minor debridement as part of routine dressing changes without recognising this as 'debridement' → define debridement clearly (sharp, mechanical, larval, enzymatic) in staff training
Out-of-hours or weekend gaps in multidisciplinary foot care service cover may lead to non-specialist staff stepping in → establish an on-call or escalation pathway for urgent debridement needs

Surgical debridement under a formal operative plan may be wrongly flagged as non-compliant → exclude debridement performed by the surgical team as part of an agreed multidisciplinary foot care service plan
Documentation may record 'wound cleaned' without specifying who did what, obscuring true practice → require role and technique to be recorded explicitly
Staff may be unaware of the restriction if it has not previously been enforced locally → communicate the standard clearly before starting data collection, to avoid appearing punitive
pearls: Provide brief training to ward nursing staff on recognising debridement and escalating to the multidisciplinary foot care service rather than proceeding themselves
Agree an urgent escalation or on-call route for debridement needs identified out of hours
Use wound photography, where available, alongside documentation to support quality review of debridement episodes
Present results supportively, focusing on system gaps (access to the specialist service) rather than individual blame
effort: ~15 min per 10 episodes from wound care documentation

question: What proportion of people with suspected acute Charcot arthropathy are referred within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day, with non-weight-bearing treatment offered in the meantime?
why: Acute Charcot arthropathy can cause severe, irreversible foot deformity if weight-bearing continues during the diagnostic delay, but the condition is easily mistaken for a simple sprain or cellulitis, delaying the urgent referral it needs. No audit of the 1-working-day Charcot referral standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.7.3 (2015)
standard.wording: To confirm the diagnosis of acute Charcot arthropathy, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day. Offer non-weight-bearing treatment until definitive treatment can be started by the multidisciplinary foot care service.

pass: Documented referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 1 working day of suspected acute Charcot arthropathy being identified, triage within 1 further working day, and non-weight-bearing advice or a device offered from the point of suspicion
population: Inclusion: adults with diabetes presenting with a red, warm, swollen or deformed foot in whom acute Charcot arthropathy is suspected. Exclusion: patients with a confirmed alternative diagnosis (for example, cellulitis or acute gout) made at first presentation
sample: 20-30 consecutive suspected acute Charcot presentations over the last 6-12 months (a low-volume but high-harm presentation)
data_source: Emergency department, podiatry, orthopaedic and diabetes clinic records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'suspected acute Charcot foot' pathway alert to the emergency department and diabetes clinic systems that triggers an immediate non-weight-bearing advice sheet and a same-day fast-track referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service.
reaudit: 6-12 months later, given the low case volume, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team meeting and emergency department governance meeting; embed the fast-track pathway alert permanently if timeliness improves.
pitfalls: Acute Charcot arthropathy is rare, making a 2-week sample impossible → extend the collection window to 6-12 months to reach a meaningful sample

The condition is commonly misdiagnosed as cellulitis or a sprain at first presentation, delaying the referral clock → audit time from first presentation with red flag features, not only from confirmed diagnosis
Non-weight-bearing advice may be given verbally without being documented → provide a printed advice sheet that is given and filed as evidence
Emergency department staff may be unfamiliar with the condition → provide a simple red-flag recognition card for diabetic foot presentations
Small numbers mean a single delayed case has a large effect on the reported percentage → present individual case narratives alongside the overall rate
pearls: Use a multi-year or multi-site case series if the local trust sees very few cases in a short window
Provide emergency department and GP education on the classic 'hot, swollen, red foot with intact skin' presentation of acute Charcot arthropathy
Keep printed non-weight-bearing advice sheets and offloading devices readily available in the emergency department
Review every case as an individual learning event with the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team, given how rare and high-harm delayed diagnosis is
effort: ~20 min per case from multi-department records

question: What proportion of people with a foot deformity resulting from previous Charcot arthropathy are under ongoing care with the foot protection service?
why: A healed Charcot foot with residual deformity remains at high, lifelong risk of new ulceration, but once the acute episode has resolved, patients can be discharged from specialist follow-up and lost to ongoing foot protection service surveillance. No audit of ongoing foot protection service care for patients with a previous Charcot deformity has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.7.8 (2015)
standard.wording: People who have a foot deformity that may be the result of a previous Charcot arthropathy are at high risk of ulceration and should be cared for by the foot protection service.

pass: Documented current, active registration with the foot protection service at high-risk review frequency for a patient with a known previous Charcot deformity
population: Inclusion: adults with a documented diagnosis of previous Charcot arthropathy and residual foot deformity. Exclusion: patients who have had a below-knee or higher amputation of the affected limb
sample: 20-30 patients with a coded history of Charcot arthropathy identified from podiatry or orthopaedic records over the last 12 months
data_source: Podiatry/foot protection service caseload records, orthopaedic and diabetes clinic letters
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Flag every confirmed Charcot arthropathy diagnosis with a permanent 'high-risk, do not discharge from foot protection service' marker on the podiatry caseload system.
target: 100% of patients with a previous Charcot deformity remaining on active foot protection service review
reaudit: 6-9 months later, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team meeting; embed the permanent high-risk marker in the podiatry caseload system if retention improves.
pitfalls: Patients may be discharged from acute Charcot follow-up once the episode resolves, without recognising ongoing high risk → make the high-risk marker permanent, distinct from acute-phase follow-up
Coding of 'Charcot arthropathy' may be inconsistent across systems, making the population hard to identify → cross-check podiatry, orthopaedic and diabetes clinic records
Patients who move house or transfer care may fall out of the local foot protection service without formal discharge being recorded → record transfer of care as a distinct category from discharge
Long time since the acute episode may mean deformity is under-recognised as Charcot-related by newer staff → ensure the permanent marker carries a clear diagnostic note
Small numbers make the percentage sensitive to a single lost-to-follow-up case → review each case individually rather than relying on the percentage alone
pearls: Use a permanent, clearly labelled flag in the podiatry electronic record rather than relying on staff memory of individual cases
Cross-reference orthopaedic, diabetes and podiatry records when building the initial case list, since Charcot patients may be seen by any of these services
Review flagged patients annually at a diabetic foot multidisciplinary team meeting to confirm ongoing appropriate review
Communicate the permanent high-risk status clearly in any discharge or transfer letter if the patient does move areas
effort: ~15 min per patient from podiatry and clinic records
